title: Lineage and a Certificate
bigQuestion: When two schools claim the same art, who has the power to say which certificate counts?

story.title: Two Frames by the Door
story.kicker: A new student notices that two rank papers on one wall trace back to two different founders.
paragraphs: A tenth grader named Dania walks into a taekwondo school in a small Illinois strip mall. She has come to sign up for Saturday classes. While the owner finds a form, Dania looks at the wall by the front desk. Two framed certificates hang side by side, each with the owner's name in large letters.

The first certificate is printed in Korean and English. At the top it says Kukkiwon, with an address in Seoul. A long registration number runs along the bottom edge. The second certificate carries a different seal and a small photo of an older man in a white uniform. Under the photo is the name Choi Hong-hi.

Dania asks why there are two. The owner laughs and says the art split into two big families in the 1960s and 1970s. One family looks to the Kukkiwon, opened in Seoul in 1972. The other looks to the International Taekwon-Do Federation, which General Choi founded in 1966. The owner says he trained under teachers from both.

Dania thinks of a family tree, where every person has two grandfathers. Each certificate is a claim about where the owner's knowledge came from. Each also names an institution that promises to stand behind that claim. She wonders which one a tournament, a college club or a court would believe.
story.think: What does a rank certificate prove, and whose promise stands behind it?

sections.title: Older Ways to Pass On an Art

lessons.title: Scrolls and Licenses
lessons.mainIdea: Older Japanese martial schools passed on authority through written licenses from a teacher, not through a national rank system.
reading: Japanese historians use the word *koryū*, meaning old-style school, for martial traditions founded before the Meiji era began in 1868. One well-known example is Tenshin Shōden Katori Shintō-ryū. The school traditionally dates its founding to the 1400s in what is now Chiba Prefecture. Each koryū keeps a list of its past headmasters, running back to a founder.

Many koryū gave students written licenses at set stages of study. The highest was often called *menkyo kaiden*, the license of complete transmission. It said the holder had received the whole curriculum of that school. Licenses were often written by hand on a *makimono*, a rolled paper scroll. The scroll named the founder and each teacher in the chain down to the student.

This system tied authority to a person, not to an office in a capital city. A license from one headmaster meant nothing inside a rival school. Arts outside the martial world worked the same way. Japanese tea schools and flower-arranging schools used a head-of-house system called iemoto, where one family controlled the right to teach and to grant licenses.

words.d: an old-style Japanese martial school founded before the Meiji era began in 1868
the license of complete transmission, the highest license in many old Japanese schools
a rolled paper scroll; many old licenses were written on one
a Japanese head-of-house system in which one family controls teaching and licenses

lessons.title: Numbered Ranks at the Kodokan
lessons.mainIdea: Kanō Jigorō gave judo numbered dan ranks in the 1880s, tying rank to an institution that keeps records.
reading: Kanō Jigorō opened the Kodokan in 1882 in a small space at Eishō-ji, a Buddhist temple in Tokyo. He had studied older jūjutsu schools that used licenses. For his new judo, he chose a different tool. In 1883 he named his first two *shodan*, or first-degree ranks: Saigō Shirō and Tomita Tsunejirō.

The word *dan* means step or grade. Players of the board game go had used dan grades in Japan since the 1600s. Kanō borrowed that idea of numbered steps. A student could rise from first dan upward, and each promotion was written in the Kodokan's records. Kyū grades, counted downward, were later used for students below first dan.

The change moved authority from a single teacher's scroll to an institution with a *registry*, a list kept over time. A Kodokan rank could be checked in Tokyo decades later. The Kodokan still issues and records dan grades today. Only a small number of people have ever received its tenth dan, the highest grade it has awarded.

words.d: a numbered step or grade of rank, used first in the game of go and later in judo
first-degree rank, the first dan
an official list kept over time, such as a record of every rank an institution has awarded

lessons.title: A National Office for Titles
lessons.mainIdea: Imperial Japan's Dai Nippon Butokukai granted martial titles from 1895 until the occupation dissolved it after 1945.
reading: In 1895 a group founded the *Dai Nippon Butokukai*, or Greater Japan Martial Virtue Association, in Kyoto. It had imperial patronage and branches across Japan. In 1899 it opened the Butokuden, a large training hall in Kyoto. Each year it held gatherings where teachers of many arts demonstrated before judges.

The Butokukai did something no single school could do. It granted national teaching titles across many arts, including kendo, judo and archery. Early in the 1900s it began awarding titles such as *hanshi* and kyōshi to senior teachers. Karate teachers from Okinawa later sought these titles too. A Butokukai title told the public that a national body had approved the holder.

The Butokukai grew closely tied to the wartime state in the 1930s and 1940s. After Japan's defeat in 1945, the Allied occupation saw it as part of that militarism. The association was dissolved in 1946. Its end showed that a body that grants titles depends on the government and laws around it.

words.d: Greater Japan Martial Virtue Association, founded in Kyoto in 1895 and dissolved in 1946
a senior teaching title granted by the Butokukai and later by other Japanese bodies
support and protection from a powerful person or family, such as an emperor

look.title: One Hall, Many Arts

look.prompt: What kind of power does a single national body gain when it grants titles across many separate arts?

choices: It merged with the Olympic movement

check.why: After 1945, the occupation dissolved the Butokukai because of its ties to the wartime state.

choices: grant national titles across many arts
keep a list of its own headmasters
check.why: As a national body, the Butokukai granted titles such as hanshi in kendo, judo, archery and other arts.

lessons.title: Funakoshi and the Shōtōkan Name
lessons.mainIdea: Funakoshi Gichin brought Okinawan karate to Tokyo in 1922, and his students later named a style after his dojo.
reading: Funakoshi Gichin was born in 1868 in Shuri, on Okinawa, the center of the old Ryukyu Kingdom. Japan had annexed the kingdom as Okinawa Prefecture in 1879. In 1922 Funakoshi gave a karate demonstration in Tokyo at an exhibition sponsored by the Ministry of Education. He stayed in Tokyo and taught in university clubs.

To fit Tokyo's martial world, Funakoshi borrowed judo's dan ranks and white uniforms. He also published books in Japanese, starting in 1922. He signed his poems with the pen name Shōtō, meaning pine waves. In 1939 his supporters opened a dojo in Tokyo and hung a sign reading *Shōtōkan*, the hall of Shōtō. United States bombing destroyed the building in 1945.

Funakoshi mostly called what he taught simply karate-dō. His students began using the name of the lost hall as the name of a *style*, a school of karate with its own lineage and forms. The sign on one building became a claim carried by clubs around the world. A style name tells people which teacher a school says it descends from.

words.d: the hall of Shōtō, Funakoshi Gichin's Tokyo dojo, opened in 1939; later the name of a karate style
a school of an art with its own lineage, forms and name
to take over a territory and make it part of another country

lessons.title: One Teacher, Several Associations
lessons.mainIdea: After Funakoshi died in 1957, groups of his students formed rival associations, and a later split went to Japanese courts.
reading: In 1949 some of Funakoshi's students founded the *Japan Karate Association*, or JKA. In 1957 Japan's Ministry of Education recognized it as a legal corporation. Funakoshi died the same year, in April 1957. Another group of his older students kept their own association, the Shotokai. Both said they carried Funakoshi's teaching forward.

The JKA trained full-time instructors and sent many abroad in the 1960s. They opened clubs in Europe, the Americas and Africa. Each instructor gave rank certificates stamped with the JKA name. Nakayama Masatoshi served as the JKA's chief instructor for decades. In this way, one Tokyo association issued rank to students on several continents.

Nakayama died in 1987. Soon after, JKA leaders split into rival groups. Each side claimed to be the true JKA, and the dispute went to Japanese courts in the 1990s. Some instructors left and formed new associations with new names. A student's certificate now depended on which group the teacher had joined.

words.d: the JKA, a karate body founded in Tokyo in 1949 by students of Funakoshi Gichin
an organized group with members, leaders and rules, often able to issue rank
an organization recognized by law as able to own property, sign contracts and go to court

look.prompt: Can two associations both be honest heirs of one teacher? What evidence would each point to?

check.why: The JKA trained professional instructors and sent them abroad, and their certificates bore the JKA name.

lessons.title: From Maeda to the Gracies
lessons.mainIdea: Brazilian jiu-jitsu grew from judo brought to Brazil by Maeda Mitsuyo, and the Gracie family made its name part of the art.
reading: Maeda Mitsuyo was a Kodokan judo student born in 1878. He left Japan in 1904 and traveled through the United States, Europe and Latin America, often in public contests. In 1914 he reached Brazil. He settled in Belém, a port city in the state of Pará, near the mouth of the Amazon River. He died there in 1941.

According to the Gracie family's account, Carlos Gracie learned from Maeda in Belém as a teenager. Carlos and his brothers later taught in Rio de Janeiro, where the family opened an academy in 1925. Historians note that Maeda also taught others in Belém, such as Luiz França. The family story is one important *lineage* claim among several.

The Gracie brothers, especially Carlos and Hélio, made their family name part of the art's identity. In 1978 Hélio's son Rorion Gracie moved to Southern California to teach. In 1993 he helped create the Ultimate Fighting Championship, whose first event was held in Denver. His brother Royce won it, and interest in *Brazilian jiu-jitsu* spread fast.

words.d: a line of teachers and students traced back through time to a founder or source
a grappling art that grew in Brazil from judo taught by Maeda Mitsuyo and others
a story of events told by a person or group, which historians compare with other evidence

choices: Belém, in the state of Pará
check.why: Maeda settled in Belém, a port near the mouth of the Amazon, and died there in 1941.

choices: Maeda also taught others in Belém, such as Luiz França

check.why: Maeda taught more than one family, so other teachers also trace their lineage to him.

check.why: Rorion Gracie helped create the UFC, whose first event was in Denver in 1993.

lessons.title: A Headquarters in Seoul
lessons.mainIdea: The Kukkiwon, opened in Seoul in 1972, issues taekwondo dan certificates that are registered and recognized worldwide.
reading: After Korea's liberation from Japanese rule in 1945, several training halls called *kwan* opened in Seoul. Among them were the Chung Do Kwan, the Moo Duk Kwan and the Jido Kwan. Each had its own founder and its own ranks. In the 1950s and 1960s, Korean leaders worked to unite the kwan under one name, taekwondo.

The South Korean government backed a central headquarters. The *Kukkiwon* opened in Seoul on November 30, 1972. In 1973 the World Taekwondo Federation was founded there to run international competition. It changed its name to World Taekwondo in 2017. The Kukkiwon kept the job of setting forms and granting dan rank.

A Kukkiwon certificate carries a registration number that can be checked against its records. Students under fifteen receive a *poom* rank instead of a dan. Many national federations in the World Taekwondo family recognize Kukkiwon rank for their black belts. That is why many schools abroad hang a Kukkiwon certificate by the door.

words.d: a Korean training hall or school; several kwan opened in Seoul after 1945
the taekwondo headquarters in Seoul, opened in 1972, which grants dan and poom rank
a Kukkiwon rank for students under fifteen, matched to dan rank

look.cite: Kukkiwon, published rules on dan and poom certification

check.why: The Kukkiwon opened in Seoul on November 30, 1972.

check.why: Under-fifteen students receive poom rank, which is matched to dan rank.

lessons.title: What a Governing Body Keeps
lessons.mainIdea: A governing body keeps rules, records and membership lists, which gives its certificates weight beyond one school.
reading: A *governing body* is an organization that sets rules for a sport and decides who may compete. In the United States, the Amateur Sports Act of 1978 set up one national governing body for each Olympic sport. It was renamed the Ted Stevens Olympic and Amateur Sports Act in 1998. USA Judo, USA Taekwondo and USA Wrestling each hold that role for their sports.

A governing body keeps things a single teacher cannot. It keeps a membership list, a rule book, a list of certified referees and a registry of rank. Its tournaments decide who goes to national and world championships. A rank from it can be checked years later, even after a local school closes.

Brazilian jiu-jitsu built its own body. The International Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu Federation, or IBJJF, was founded in 2002 by Carlos Gracie Jr. It registers black belts and sets minimum ages for adult belts. Under its rules, a person must be at least nineteen to receive a black belt. A school that wants its students in IBJJF events follows those rules.

words.d: an organization that sets rules for a sport and decides who may compete
a 1978 U.S. law that set up one national governing body for each Olympic sport
the youngest age at which a rule allows a person to hold a rank or enter an event

lessons.title: Two Taekwondo Families
lessons.mainIdea: Choi Hong-hi's International Taekwon-Do Federation grew apart from the Kukkiwon, so taekwondo has two major lines of rank.
reading: Choi Hong-hi was a South Korean army general who taught martial arts to soldiers in the 1950s. He was part of the group that chose the name taekwondo in 1955. In 1966 he founded the *International Taekwon-Do Federation*, or ITF, in Seoul. He wrote its forms and its rules.

Choi fell out with South Korea's government in the early 1970s. In 1972 he moved the ITF's headquarters to Toronto, Canada. He later brought ITF teachers to North Korea. Meanwhile, the Kukkiwon and the World Taekwondo Federation grew in Seoul with state support. Taekwondo became an Olympic demonstration sport in 1988, and a full medal sport in 2000 under World Taekwondo rules.

Choi died in 2002 in Pyongyang. After his death, the ITF split into several groups, each with its own president and certificates. So a taekwondo *black belt* can come from the Kukkiwon line or from one of several ITF lines. The forms, the scoring rules and the names on the certificates differ between the families.

words.d: the ITF, founded in Seoul in 1966 by Choi Hong-hi and later moved to Toronto
the belt worn by holders of first dan and above in many modern martial arts
a sport shown at the Olympic Games without counting in the official medal table

lessons.title: A Family Name as a Mark
lessons.mainIdea: Trademark law lets a business own a name for its services, which turned the Gracie family name into a legal question.
reading: A *trademark* is a word, name or symbol that tells buyers who is selling a product or service. In the United States, the Lanham Act of 1946 is the main federal trademark law. A business can register a mark with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office. The owner can then sue others who use the mark in a way that confuses buyers.

After moving to California, Rorion Gracie registered the name Gracie Jiu-Jitsu as a trademark. But the Gracie family was large, and many relatives taught under their own name. In the 1990s, family members took disputes over the name to U.S. federal courts. The question was whether one branch could own the family name as a mark for teaching.

The Gracie cases show a clash between two kinds of authority. Lineage says a name belongs to everyone taught in a line. Trademark law says a name belongs to whoever registers and uses it in trade. A *federal court* decides these cases under statutes, not under the customs of a school.

words.d: a word, name or symbol that shows who sells a product or service; it can be registered and protected by law
the main U.S. federal trademark law, passed in 1946
a U.S. national court that decides cases under federal laws such as the Lanham Act

lessons.title: Generic Words and Protected Names
lessons.mainIdea: Common art names cannot be owned, but some names, such as Olympic and Shaolin, are protected by law or registration.
reading: Trademark law does not let anyone own a *generic term*, the everyday name for a kind of thing. Words like karate, judo and taekwondo name whole arts. Any school may put them on its sign. A school can only register its own distinct name, such as a family name joined to a style.

Some names get special protection. The Amateur Sports Act gives the U.S. Olympic Committee the exclusive right to use the word Olympic in the United States. In 1987 the U.S. Supreme Court upheld that right in San Francisco Arts and Athletics v. United States Olympic Committee. A group had planned to call its event the Gay Olympic Games and was stopped.

Temples can register names too. Since the late 1990s, the Shaolin Temple in Dengfeng, Henan Province, has registered its name as a trademark in China and many other countries. The temple is linked in legend to Bodhidharma and to the start of Chinese boxing, stories historians treat as legend. Today its *registration* lets it act in court over who may use the name.

words.d: the everyday name for a kind of thing, which no one can own as a trademark
official recording of a trademark with a government office, which helps the owner defend it in court
a right that belongs to one person or group and no one else
